title: Age-related macular degeneration (drusen): central scotoma
vignette: A 65-year-old man comes to the office due to vision difficulties. He says his eyesight has gotten progressively worse over the past year. The fundus of the patient's left eye is shown in the exhibit, which reveals yellowish deposits of lipids and calcium (drusen) clustered around the macula. Which of the following defects is most likely to be revealed by visual field testing?

clues.text: eyesight has gotten progressively worse over the past year
clues.note: Gradual, progressive CENTRAL vision loss in an older adult suggests a macular process.

clues.text: yellowish deposits of lipids and calcium (drusen) clustered around the macula
clues.note: DRUSEN (yellow subretinal deposits) around the macula are the hallmark of age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

whatMatters: Drusen clustered around the MACULA = age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Because the macula subserves CENTRAL, high-acuity vision, macular damage produces a CENTRAL SCOTOMA (a central visual-field defect). Answer D. AMD is the leading cause of blindness in patients >50.
strategy: Localize by the affected retinal region: the MACULA (central retina, dense cones/fovea) mediates central acuity, so its degeneration causes a CENTRAL scotoma. Reject defects from other locations: arcuate scotoma (glaucoma - nerve-fiber bundle/optic nerve), binasal/bitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm), and homonymous hemianopia (retrochiasmal/optic tract) - none produces fundoscopic drusen.

eliminations.label: Arcuate scotoma - glaucoma (nerve fiber layer)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an arc-shaped defect extending from the blind spot, following retinal nerve-fiber bundles - classic for glaucoma. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it reflects optic-nerve/nerve-fiber damage (with increased cup-to-disc ratio), not macular drusen. ✅ Correct if: glaucoma with optic cupping and peripheral loss.

eliminations.label: Binasal hemianopia - lateral chiasm compression
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: loss of the nasal fields of both eyes, from compression of the LATERAL optic chiasm bilaterally. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is a chiasmal defect, not a macular one, and the fundus would be normal. ✅ Correct if: bilateral lateral chiasm compression.

eliminations.label: Bitemporal hemianopia - central chiasm (pituitary)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: loss of the temporal fields of both eyes from compression of the crossing fibers at the optic chiasm (e.g., pituitary adenoma). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is chiasmal with a normal fundus, not the macular drusen picture. ✅ Correct if: a pituitary/chiasmal lesion.

eliminations.label: Homonymous hemianopia - retrochiasmal lesion
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: loss of the same-side field in both eyes, from an optic tract/radiation/occipital lesion. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it localizes behind the chiasm and doesn't change the fundus appearance. ✅ Correct if: a retrochiasmal (stroke/tumor) lesion.

reasoning: Drusen clustered around the macula = age-related macular degeneration
The macula (fovea) provides central, high-acuity vision
Macular degeneration therefore causes loss of the central visual field
mechanism: The MACULA is the central retina, densely packed with cone photoreceptors (with a 1:1 cone-to-ganglion arrangement at the fovea) that provide the sharpest CENTRAL VISION. AGE-RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION (AMD) primarily damages the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which normally nourishes photoreceptors and clears their waste; with RPE dysfunction, waste products accumulate as yellow subretinal DRUSEN, and the overlying macular photoreceptors degenerate. Loss of macular function produces a CENTRAL SCOTOMA - a defect in the center of the visual field with relatively preserved peripheral vision - which impairs reading and face recognition. AMD is the leading cause of blindness in people over 50 (dry/atrophic form is most common; wet/neovascular form involves choroidal neovascularization). A scotoma is a discrete, usually monocular field defect; the distractor patterns localize to the optic nerve (arcuate - glaucoma) or the visual pathway at/behind the chiasm (bitemporal, binasal, homonymous) and would not show macular drusen.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Ophtho > age-related macular degeneration: drusen (RPE dysfunction), central scotoma, central vision loss; leading cause of blindness >50; dry (atrophic) vs wet (neovascular).

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Macular (central) damage -> central scotoma; drusen confirm AMD.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on macula/fovea, drusen, retinal pigment epithelium, scotoma, or hemianopia patterns? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Arcuate scotoma = glaucoma; bitemporal/binasal = chiasm; homonymous = retrochiasmal - none has macular drusen.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.text: On the fundus photo: yellow subretinal deposits (drusen) clustered around the central macula. Anchor: 'macular drusen = AMD = central scotoma.'

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: AMD = drusen at macula -> central scotoma; leading cause of blindness >50; wet form = anti-VEGF.

keywords.front: Visual field defect in macular disease

keywords.back: Most common cause of blindness in patients >50

firstAid.detail: Ophtho: drusen at macula -> central scotoma; RPE dysfunction.

memoryHook: Drusen bury the macula - the eye's central 'HD camera' - so the middle of vision blacks out: a central scotoma of macular degeneration.
